Q: Does Jax's JIT compiler unroll for loops inside if statements that are not executed? A:

I don't know the answer to your question, but I don't think that the motivation for asking it is sound. It boils down to this:

"Unrolling the loop would be undesirable because it could massively increase the compile time."

  1. JIT compile time should be irrelevant. The code should be compiled once and then executed many times. If you are repeatedly JIT compiling the same code multiple times, something is wrong: doing that would be inefficient.

  2. The cost of JIT compilation (of an unrolled loop) shouldn't be "massive".

  3. If (in spite of 1 and 2) there is a real (i.e. you have measured it!) performance issue here, then there is a simple work-around. Tune your code. In your example, you could move the for loop into a separate function, and JIT compile it separately ... or not.

Before you try 3, make sure that you understand how to measure your application properly (the jax.jit documentation uses timeit in its examples) and methodically do before and after tests for each tuning tweak that you make.

Also, be aware that the behavior of the JIT compiler could be version dependent, and you may need to redo the tuning.

Having said the above, as I was reading the jax.jit documentation, I came across this section:

  • https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/jit-compilation.html#why-can-t-we-just-jit-everything

You should read that carefully. In that it says:

"Traced values within JIT, like x and n here, can only affect control flow via their static attributes: such as shape or dtype, and not via their values.)

I think that means that in your example where do_the_loop is a runtime variable, the JIT compiler would not take account of value of that variable in deciding whether or not to unroll the loop.

But as I said above, I don't think it matters. Time to JIT compile should not have a significant bearing on overall performance ... if you are using it correctly.

Q: Why do Google Analytics 4 (GA4) network calls fire on "stackoverflow.com" even after turning off the cookies from the OneTrust Cookie settings? A:

A:

GA4 network calls appearing on sites like Stack Overflow can happen for several technical reasons—even when you think tracking is disabled. Here are the key explanations:

1. GA4 Is Embedded by the Website

Stack Overflow itself uses GA4 as part of its analytics setup. So when you visit the site, your browser loads GA4 scripts (like gtag.js) directly from their servers.

  • This happens regardless of your own GA4 settings (those only affect your website, not others).

  • You’re seeing outbound requests initiated by Stack Overflow, not your configuration.

2. Consent Mode and Limited Tracking

Even if you decline cookies via a consent banner:

  • GA4 may still send “cookieless pings”

  • These are anonymized signals used for modeling (not full tracking)

This is part of Google Analytics 4 Consent Mode, designed to balance privacy with measurement.

3. Ad Blockers Don’t Always Block Everything

Extensions or browser protections may:

  • Block some GA requests (like collect)

  • But allow others (like g/collect or regional endpoints)

Reasons include:

  • Updated GA endpoints not yet blacklisted

  • Partial blocking rules

  • First-party proxying (harder to detect)

4. First-Party Proxying or Server-Side Tracking

Some sites route GA4 data through their own domain (server-side tracking):

  • This makes requests look like they’re coming from the same site

  • Many blockers don’t catch these

5. Browser DevTools Show Attempted Calls

Even if a request is blocked:

  • It may still appear in the Network tab as “failed” or “blocked”

  • This can give the impression GA4 is still “firing”

6. Cached Scripts or Service Workers

Previously loaded scripts or service workers may:

  • Continue triggering background requests

  • Especially in modern web apps like Stack Overflow

7. You Can’t Control Third-Party GA4 Behavior

Turning off GA4 in your own property:

  • Does not affect other websites

  • Each site independently controls its analytics setup

How to Verify What’s Really Happening

To confirm:

  • Check request status (200 vs blocked)

  • Look at request domains (google-analytics.com, custom domains)

  • Disable extensions and compare behavior

  • Use stricter tools like browser-level tracking protection

Conclusion

GA4 calls on Stack Overflow are normal because the site uses its own analytics implementation. Even with blockers or consent restrictions, limited or attempted requests may still appear due to consent mode, proxying, or partial blocking.

Q: How to detect support for the proposed `_split` window target? A:

Per the explainer you linked to a new navigator.splitTabSupported boolean is supposed to be added.
You should be able to check for its presence to know whether that value is supported by the UA or not.

console.log("knows about split tab?", "splitTabSupported" in navigator);
console.log("currently supported", !!navigator.splitTabSupported);

Note that both checks don't do the same, since when an UA knows about _split, but doesn't support it in the current context, it should treat it as _blank.
